title: Multiple dispatch and method specificity
outcome: Design generic operations over owned types and resolve overlapping method signatures explicitly.
key_terms: Julia selects a method using the runtime types of all positional arguments, not only the first one.
A type that cannot be instantiated and groups concrete types, so one method can serve a whole family of them.
When several methods apply, Julia calls the one whose signature is more specific than every other applicable signature.
An error raised when two applicable methods are each more specific in a different argument and neither is chosen.
Adding a method to a function you do not own for argument types you do not own, which can change behavior in unrelated code.
approach: Dispatch chooses a method from the types of all positional arguments, while each constructor still checks its own numeric domain. `Circle` and `Rectangle` accept finite nonnegative sizes, `area` has one method per shape, and `classify` has two one-sided integer methods plus an explicit `(Integer, Integer)` method that resolves their overlap.

exercises.title: Add a zero-size shape
exercises.hint: Check the boundary without rejecting a valid degenerate shape.
exercises.answer: The constructor permits nonnegative dimensions, including zero.
exercises.why: Radius 0 satisfies `stored >= 0`, so `Circle(0)` is valid and `pi * 0^2` is 0.
exercises.wrong: Rejecting zero as if it were negative removes a legitimate degenerate case and makes empty shapes impossible to represent.

exercises.title: Reject an invalid dimension
exercises.hint: Dispatch does not replace domain validation.
exercises.answer: A method for the right type can still receive scientifically invalid values unless its contract prevents them.
exercises.why: `Rectangle(1, -1)` fails `h >= 0`, so the constructor throws `ArgumentError` even though the argument types are valid reals.
exercises.wrong: Relying on the `Real` type annotation to block bad sizes misses that -1 is a perfectly good `Real`.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `@test_throws ArgumentError Rectangle(1, -1)` and the same for `Circle(-1)`.

exercises.title: Trace both arguments
exercises.task: Call classify with an integer in each position separately.
exercises.expected: Different methods handle the two cases.
exercises.hint: Method selection uses the positional type tuple.
exercises.answer: There is no requirement that one argument be a special receiver.
exercises.why: `classify(1, "x")` matches only `(Integer, Any)` and `classify("x", 1)` matches only `(Any, Integer)`, so they return different symbols.
exercises.wrong: Reasoning as in single-dispatch languages, where only the first argument selects behavior, predicts the same method for both calls.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `:first_integer` and `:second_integer` for these two calls.

exercises.title: Resolve the overlap
exercises.expected: The explicit intersection method is selected.
exercises.hint: Neither one-sided signature alone expresses the complete overlap rule.
exercises.answer: An intersection method documents behavior and prevents ambiguity.
exercises.why: Both one-sided methods match `(1, 2)`, and neither is more specific; the `(Integer, Integer)` method is more specific than both and is chosen.
exercises.wrong: Deleting the intersection method to simplify the code turns `classify(1, 2)` into a `MethodError` reporting ambiguity.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `classify(1, 2) == :both_integers`; `methods(classify)` lists all three signatures.

exercises.title: Keep an unsupported case visible
exercises.task: Pass two floating-point values to classify.
exercises.answer: A catch-all fallback should be added only when its semantics are defined.
exercises.why: `(1.0, 2.0)` matches none of the three signatures, so Julia raises `MethodError` rather than guessing a result.
exercises.wrong: Adding `classify(a, b) = :other` to silence the error claims a meaning for float pairs that the design never defined.

exercises.title: Extend an owned interface
exercises.task: Sketch another Shape subtype and an area method.
exercises.expected: The generic total can use the operation if its laws hold.
exercises.hint: An abstract type does not implement the behavior itself.
exercises.answer: Test the new method and invariants rather than assuming subtype membership proves interface correctness.
exercises.why: A new `struct Square <: Shape` with an `area` method lets `total_area` include it, because the sum only calls `area` on each element.
exercises.wrong: Declaring the subtype without an `area` method compiles, but `total_area` then fails with `MethodError` at the first square.
exercises.verify: Test the new `area` on a known side length and include it in a `Shape[]` passed to `total_area`.

checks_note: Zero-size shapes are allowed, so `Circle(0)` and `Rectangle(0, 5)` both have area 0, while negative radius or height fails in the inner constructor with `ArgumentError`. The subtype line shows `Circle <: Shape`, and the concreteness check explains why: `Circle` can be instantiated with fields, while `Shape` is an abstract node that only groups methods. A new shape must define its own `area` method to join the dispatch table.
